title: Clement Hofbauer (15 March)
hook: a baker's apprentice turned priest who helped renew the Church in Vienna

segments.voice: Yesterday, Frances of Rome, who closed her prayer book again and again to answer a call. Your line was she left prayer to serve. How did the interruptions go? Day nine hundred seventy-five.

Bread can't be hurried. Flour, water, yeast, and then the long wait, the dough sitting under a cloth doing work nobody can see. A baker learns to get up in the dark, do what can be done, and then leave the rest alone. Clement Hofbauer learned that trade as a young man in Moravia, in central Europe. He wanted to be a priest, but his family was poor, so he kneaded dough instead. It would be years before anything he hoped for began to rise. Today is about him, and about slow work.
screen: `BREAD CAN'T BE HURRIED.` → `A BAKER'S APPRENTICE IN MORAVIA.` → `A HOPE THAT TAKES YEARS TO RISE.`

segments.voice: Clement's road was long and crooked. He worked in a monastery bakery, tried life as a hermit, walked to Rome as a pilgrim, and finally, with help from generous strangers, studied for the priesthood. In Rome he joined the Redemptorists, a young order of preachers, and was sent north to Warsaw. There he and his companions threw themselves into a city church: preaching, confessions, a school, a home for orphans. A story is told about him from those years. He went into a tavern to beg for his orphans, and a man spat in his face. Clement wiped it off and said, more or less, that was for me, now what will you give for my orphans? The man was so shaken, the story goes, that he gave. Then the political tide turned. The Warsaw community was shut down and the priests sent away. Clement ended up in Vienna, chaplain to a convent of nuns, hearing confessions and talking with students, artists and writers who came to his rooms. Little of it looked like success. But those conversations helped renew Catholic life in the city, and he is now remembered as a patron of Vienna. The Letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims, describes this kind of patience: "Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth." A baker's version would be: the dough is rising, even if you can't see it. Clement didn't live to see his order firmly planted in Austria. It came after him.
screen: `A LONG, CROOKED ROAD TO THE PRIESTHOOD.` · `WARSAW: ORPHANS, AND A SPAT-ON FACE.` · `SHUT DOWN, SENT TO VIENNA.` · `CONVERSATIONS THAT RENEWED A CITY.` · then, large: `THE HUSBANDMAN WAITETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with slow work. Settle, and breathe. Find one thing in your life that isn't rising as fast as you'd like. A project. A habit. A child learning something. A friendship that's still shy. Your own healing. Picture it like dough under a cloth: you've done your part, and now there's work going on that you can't see. Resist the urge to poke it. If you pray, you can hand it to God for today. If you don't, just breathe, and let it rise without you for a while. The bell holds the time.
Clement Hofbauer. A baker's apprentice who became a Redemptorist priest, cared for orphans in Warsaw, and helped renew the Church in Vienna.

howItsDone: Catholics keep 15 March as the feast of Saint Clement Mary Hofbauer, especially in Vienna, where he is a patron of the city, and among the Redemptorists, who honor him as a founder of their work north of the Alps.
